title: The map that turned Rat Twitter into neighborhoods
summary:
The funniest part is how a nerdy Gephi follower-graph project accidentally became a whole identity system: @euxenus starts with “broke: Twitter algo / bespoke: directly perusing follower graph,” then ends up basically handing rationalist/postrat Twitter a literal map to point at and say “that’s my people.” The whole thing runs on a DIY recipe—pull followers via the Twitter API, modularity clustering, ForceAtlas2—and then the real game is everyone arguing over what the colors *mean*.

Arc-wise: Jan 2020 is @euxenus posting early graphs and openly squinting at them (“communities are hard to distinguish for me”), trying to label blobs like “pink: rationalists,” “green: weird rationalists / ‘postrationalists’,” “blue: buddhist-ish.” People jump in with competing taxonomies: @eigenrobot says the divides are “based on secondary/off-twitter media,” while @frideswyth goes full vibes-based classification (“Red: earnest shitposters / Green: unapologetic shitposters / Blue: surfers of The Weirding”), and even @eigenrobot replies “Pink?????” like, yeah, good luck pinning that down. The peak is May 2020 when @euxenus ships the artifact: Twitterverse’s interactive “Rats, etc” supergraph (twitterverse.net), and then starts naming who’s “central” in what cluster—e.g. calling @literalbanana, @eigenrobot, and @sonyasupposedly “core postrat” (dark tangerine) and pointing out “weird-sun” accounts as a big anchoring blob (dodger blue). That’s when it turns social: @DanielleFong celebrates that “people I love the most are in my neighbourhood,” pings people as “network neighbours,” and the thing becomes a tool for finding friends, not just doing analysis.

After that, it diffuses into memes: by 2021 you’ve got @mechanical_monk doing the “rationalist on postrat twitter” bit (“aargh what does that even MEAN”) and replies like “it’s just vibes bro” (@m_ashcroft) and “textures of meaningness” (@GeniesLoki). By 2022 “post-rationalist twitter” is literally a Midjourney prompt (@chercher_ai), which is the moment you realize the label escaped and became aesthetic. And then the ending is the most Twitter possible: 2023 nostalgia + platform decay—@goblinodds wonders what the chart would look like now, and @euxenus shrugs that with API changes “only God (and Elon) knows.” Why care: it’s a clean case study of how a tool that’s “just a graph” turns into a mirror a scene uses to define itself… right up until the platform pulls the plug.
